sources.citation: Baker, Brett, Mark Donohue & Janet Fletcher. 2020/2021. Australia and New Guinea. Ch. 26 in C. Gussenhoven & A. Chen (eds), The Oxford Handbook of Language Prosody, 383-395. Oxford: OUP. Author accepted manuscript, Minerva Access hdl 11343/275209.
sources.note: sec. 26.4.1 (AAM p. 8; published p. 391): 'One [Torricelli; Sandaun, PNG] regularly assigns stress to the penultimate syllable, but verbs allow for stress on either syllable of the final foot, resulting in contrasts such as [ˈte.re] chop and [te.ˈre] howl.. *[te.ˈli] with final stress is not a possible noun.' Generic 'One' = Donohue's field variety, Molmo One (Donohue 2000 fn.1); not attributed to Inebu One.

sources.citation: Donohue, Mark. 2007. Lexicography for your friends. In J. Siegel, J. Lynch & D. Eades (eds), Language Description, History and Development: Linguistic indulgence in memory of Terry Crowley (CLL 30), 395-405. Amsterdam: Benjamins. doi:10.1075/cll.30.37don
sources.note: Author's copy via the Internet Archive (papuan.linguistics.anu.edu.au). About the Molmo One community dictionary (Sikale, Crowther & Donohue 2001); no occurrence of stress, accent, tone, syllable or Inebu in the text.
Phonology section gives Molmo One segments (from Foley 2018) only; Inebu One appears only as a ward location; cites Crowther 2001 for dialectology. No stress.

sources.citation: Donohue, Mark & Melissa Crowther. 2005. Meeting in the middle: interaction in North-Central New Guinea. In A. Pawley, R. Attenborough, J. Golson & R. Hide (eds), Papuan Pasts (Pacific Linguistics 572), 167-184. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: The only source with Inebu One data: pp.178-179 twelve Inebu lexemes in a Romei/Inebu/Siama comparison; p.180 Table 2 Inebu consonants p t m n f s w l y; p.181 Table 3 vowels i e ɛ a o u; p.181: 'Tonal systems are consistently absent in the Torricelli languages (relevant here are the One varieties)'; p.182 Table 4 'Comparative suprasegmental inventories': Inebu row empty (no pitch contrasts). Nothing at all on stress placement.

tone.quote: Tonal systems are consistently absent in the Torricelli languages (relevant here are the One varieties), and the western languages (Sentani, Tobati, Ningera). The tonal systems in the phonologies of the Skou family languages are completely dominant, and remarkably comparable (Donohue 2003). Tonality in the Serra Hills languages varies inversely with their distance from the Skou languages, suggesting that tone is an areal phenomenon supported by the simple syllable-based tone systems of the Skou languages.
tone.says: States that tonal systems are absent in the Torricelli languages including the One varieties; Table 4 (p.182) 'Comparative suprasegmental inventories' lists One (Siama, Inebu, Romei) with no pitch contrasts, against H/L/F/R systems in the neighbouring Piore River and Serra Hills languages and the Skou family; tone treated as an areal feature radiating from Skou that does not reach One.
